title: J. Paul Getty Museum: Masterpieces
subtitle: Twenty paintings in which appearances are arranged, interrupted or closely examined.
introduction:
A laugh and a yawn are awkward things to hold for a portrait. Rembrandt and Ducreux make them the subject, allowing expressions usually excluded from a public likeness to take over. Elsewhere in this selection, an enormous red garment or a carefully furnished terrace gives a sitter the composure those self-portraits refuse.

The contrast is not simply between honesty and pretence. An apparently spontaneous expression is still painted and arranged; ceremonial dress can reveal a social role with considerable precision. These twenty works from the Getty offer ways to distinguish the person, the presentation and the setting. Landscapes and still lifes extend the question: what has been selected for display, and what remains just outside it?
visitNote: This selection concerns paintings in the J. Paul Getty Museum collection. Check the Getty’s current object pages for display locations and loans. Reproductions retain their source frames or calibration borders where present; these are outside the painted image.

works.description: Rembrandt tips his head back in an expression that seems difficult to sustain. The short, uneven strokes support the impression of movement, while the metal gorget supplies a more formal costume. Painted on a small copper plate around 1628, this self-portrait brings performance and observation together. The apparent passing moment is the result of a very deliberate painted arrangement.

works.title: Christ's Entry into Brussels in 1889
works.credit: James Ensor. Christ's Entry Into Brussels in 1889. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.license: Public domain (WikiArt label)
works.description: Banners and emphatic faces press forward until the figure named in the title becomes difficult to find. Ensor makes a public arrival compete with the crowd's appetite for its own spectacle. Masks offer no simple distinction between disguise and ordinary faces. The painting asks where attention goes when everyone appears determined to command it.

works.description: The flags mark a public celebration, but the man on crutches at the near edge cannot be absorbed into a simple image of prosperity. Getty identifies the occasion as the national holiday of 30 June 1878. Manet places different conditions of life within the same street. The amputee may have been a veteran; the image alone cannot establish his history.

works.description: The stacks give Monet's changing light something stable to describe. Their dark masses remain legible while blue and pink shadows spread across the snow around them. What might otherwise be dismissed as a repeated rural subject becomes a way of measuring differences. The title's season and time are not decorative additions: they identify conditions central to this particular appearance.

works.description: The instruments belong to one kind of coordinated activity; the pushing hands and striking bodies have turned towards another. La Tour compresses the group until there is little room around the quarrel. Faces and gestures must explain the interruption. Keeping the instruments in view matters, because they make the broken possibility of a shared performance part of the fight.

works.description: The letter gives the two sitters something to share beyond their place on the seat. David draws their bodies close while their contrasting clothes keep them distinct. A double portrait has to negotiate exactly that balance: two recognisable people and a visible relationship. Here a small sheet of paper connects the posed group to someone or something beyond the frame.

works.title: Self-Portrait, Yawning
works.credit: Joseph Ducreux. Self-portrait, yawning. Image: WikiArt. Public domain (WikiArt label). Proportionally resized and JPEG compressed; no crop.
works.license: Public domain (WikiArt label)
works.description: Ducreux lets a yawn take possession of the whole upper body. The extended arms pull at his clothes; the open mouth refuses the composed expression expected of a formal sitter. Yet this bodily reflex is also a choice about self-presentation. The portrait demonstrates how convincingly an artist can stage the moment when dignified control appears to lapse.

works.description: The reclining pose takes possession of a furnished terrace rather than merely occupying a chair. Winterhalter distributes light across the pale dress and surrounds the sitter with drapery, plants and distant space. Leisure becomes visible as an extensive arrangement of property and comfort. The face is only one part of the evidence through which this portrait establishes rank.

works.title: Maria Frederike van Reede-Athlone at Seven Years of Age
works.catalogueTitle: Portrait of Maria Frederike van Reede-Athlone at Seven Years of Age
works.credit: Jean-Étienne Liotard. Portrait of Maria Frederike van Reede-Athlone at Seven Years of Age. WikiArt source label: Public domain. Proportional resize and JPEG compression; no crop. Source: https://www.wikiart.org/en/jean-etienne-liotard/portrait-of-maria-frederike-van-reede-athlone-at-seven-years-of-age-1756
works.license: Public domain (WikiArt source label)
works.description: The small dog gives the child's hands something living to hold amid the carefully arranged ribbons, bonnet and fur. Liotard distinguishes these textures without allowing costume to swallow the sitter. The turned face remains particular. Formal dress establishes how the child is presented, while the animal introduces a weight and a relationship that the clothing alone cannot provide.

works.title: Alfonso d'Avalos in Armour with a Page
works.catalogueTitle: Portrait of Alfonso d`Avalos , in Armor with a Page
works.credit: Portrait of Alfonso d`Avalos , in Armor with a Page. WikiArt; Titian. Proportional resizing and JPEG compression; source frame preserved.
works.license: Public domain
works.description: Curved metal catches the light differently from the sitter's face, making armour a substantial presence rather than a shorthand label for military rank. Titian places the smaller page beside him, giving authority a human relationship as well as material equipment. The portrait's hierarchy is therefore visible before any biography is read: one man is presented, while another attends to him.

works.description: The red garment expands across much of the lower painting, almost becoming the sitter's architecture. Van Dyck brings the pale face and hands out above this ceremonial weight. Costume does not merely decorate an otherwise independent likeness. It establishes how the body occupies space, and how an individual can appear before the viewer as the bearer of an office.

works.description: Hoffmann gives the hare a principal figure's place, then continues the close attention into leaves, bark and smaller creatures. The animal does not stand before a conveniently empty backdrop. The surrounding detail makes looking a matter of moving between different scales: the hare's body first, then the particular things among which that body has been placed.

works.description: The ark supplies a destination for a gathering that could not be observed as an ordinary landscape. Brueghel spreads different species across trees and open ground, making their distinct bodies available for comparison. The biblical narrative gives this variety a reason to share the same space. Looking can move from creature to creature without losing the event that joins them.

works.description: The reclining woman is displayed above an assembled crowd, whose attention defines her role in the scene. Cézanne's abrupt colour and awkward forms deny the arrangement a polished elegance. The title is broad, but the painting presents a specific imbalance: one figure is exposed to many observers. Their looking is as much a subject as the body they inspect.

works.title: Hunting on the Lagoon
works.credit: Vittore Carpaccio. Hunting on the Lagoon. WikiArt source label: Public domain. Proportional resize and JPEG compression; no crop. Source: https://www.wikiart.org/en/vittore-carpaccio/hunting-on-the-lagoon
works.license: Public domain (WikiArt source label)
works.description: Open water keeps the small actions in Carpaccio's boats from obscuring one another. Figures stand and aim, while birds, poles and the low horizon punctuate the distance. The hunt unfolds through dispersed attention rather than one decisive confrontation. Its measured arrangement lets the observer follow separate activities across a field that remains remarkably calm.

works.description: The large pale doors establish the girl's smallness before her age is known. Khnopff gives her a precise position against their nearly empty surface, with one hand drawn towards her chest. The architecture makes her stillness conspicuous, but it does not explain her feelings. It is enough to observe how a modest figure holds attention within so much unoccupied space.

works.description: Dark dress and a pale mantilla establish a formal public appearance, but Goya does not allow that appearance to erase the sitter's particular face. The full-length pose extends her presence into the landscape behind. Social standing is clear; personality is less easily named. The portrait gives evidence to examine rather than a ready verdict about the woman represented.

works.description: The title preserves the model's name rather than leaving him an anonymous type. Géricault concentrates light on the forehead, cheek and open collar, holding the turned head against darkness. A study can attend to someone as an individual even when it belongs to a painter's wider working practice. Here the face does not need a larger scene to justify sustained attention.

works.description: The woman's arms keep the winged child away, giving the allegory an immediately readable action. Bouguereau's smooth finish makes the crossing limbs and drapery easy to follow. Cupid establishes that the encounter is an invention about love, not an observed garden incident. The scene's playfulness depends on a controlled contest of gestures rather than on uncertainty about what is happening.

works.description: Chardin places reflective metal beside fruit and hard shells without turning the ledge into a display of abundance. The restrained tones make small material differences consequential. Grapes trail towards the edge, loosening the arrangement without undoing it. After the elaborate costumes and public spectacles in this selection, a handful of objects offers a quieter test of how attention is directed.

closingSections.title: Compare what the setting supplies
paragraphs: Place a formal portrait beside one of the expressive self-portraits. Which parts of the person's appearance depend on clothes, furniture or the gesture chosen? Then try the question on the still life. These works form a study selection; consult current Getty records and visiting information before treating any of them as a stop on a physical route.
